First plug in \(x=0\):

\[
f(0)-1999f(0)=18
\]

so

\[
-1998f(0)=18
\]

and therefore

\[
f(0)=-\frac{1}{111}.
\]

Now define

\[
g(x)=f(x)+\frac{1}{111}.
\]

Then \(g\) is continuous, \(g(0)=0\), and substituting into the equation gives

\[
g(x)-1999g(T(x))=0
\]

for \(|x|\ne 1\). Hence

\[
g(x)=1999g(T(x)).
\]

For any real number \(y\), choose

\[
x=\tan\left(\frac12 \arctan y\right).
\]

Then \(x\in(-1,1)\), so \(|x|\ne 1\), and by the double-angle identity,

\[
T(x)=\frac{2x}{1-x^2}=\tan(\arctan y)=y.
\]

Thus, for every real \(y\),

\[
g\left(\tan\left(\frac12 \arctan y\right)\right)=1999g(y).
\]

Let

\[
h(y)=\tan\left(\frac12 \arctan y\right).
\]

Then

\[
h^n(y)=\tan\left(\frac{1}{2^n}\arctan y\right),
\]

and as \(n\to\infty\),

\[
h^n(y)\to 0.
\]

From the relation above,

\[
g(y)=\frac{g(h(y))}{1999}
      =\frac{g(h^2(y))}{1999^2}
      =\cdots
      =\frac{g(h^n(y))}{1999^n}.
\]

Since \(g\) is continuous and \(g(0)=0\),

\[
g(h^n(y))\to g(0)=0.
\]

Therefore,

\[
g(y)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{g(h^n(y))}{1999^n}=0.
\]

This holds for every real \(y\), so \(g\equiv 0\). Hence

\[
f(x)+\frac{1}{111}=0
\]

for all \(x\), i.e.

\[
f(x)=-\frac{1}{111}.
\]

A quick check confirms it works:

\[
-\frac{1}{111}-1999\left(-\frac{1}{111}\right)
=\frac{1998}{111}=18.
\]

Thus the unique continuous solution is

\[
\boxed{f(x)=-\frac{1}{111}}.
\]

27B·v4.method: Evaluate at x=0 for particular solution; subtract to get homogeneous equation; use inverse branch H(y)=tan(½arctan y) to iterate backward, showing g≡0 by continuity at 0.
